p.src: After reading articles of this kind, I gradually grew depressed at the thought of remaining in this country and resolved somehow to return to the land of us human beings. But no matter how long I searched, I could not find the hole through which I had fallen. Before long, the fisherman kappa Bag told me that an elderly kappa supposedly lived quietly on the outskirts of a town in this country, reading books and playing the flute. I thought that if I asked this kappa, he might perhaps know a way to escape from the country, so I immediately set out for the outskirts of town. Yet when I arrived, instead of an elderly kappa, I found in the very small house a kappa of barely twelve or thirteen, whose head-plate had not even hardened, leisurely playing the flute. Naturally, I thought I must have entered the wrong house. But when, to make sure, I asked his name, he proved to be none other than the elderly kappa Bag had told me about. “But you look like a child…” “Don’t you know yet? By some twist of fate, I already had a head of white hair when I came out of my mother’s womb. Since then I have gradually grown younger, until now I have become a child like this. Still, if you count my age, taking me to have been sixty before birth, I may now be around a hundred and fifteen or sixteen.” I looked around the room. Perhaps it was only my imagination, but amid the plain chairs and table there seemed to hover a kind of pure happiness. “You seem to live more happily than the other kappas, don’t you?” “Well, perhaps that is so. When I was young, I was old; and now that I am old, I have become young.

But no matter how long I searched, I could not find the hole through which I had fallen.
Before long, the fisherman kappa Bag told me that an elderly kappa supposedly lived quietly on the outskirts of a town in this country, reading books and playing the flute.
I thought that if I asked this kappa, he might perhaps know a way to escape from the country, so I immediately set out for the outskirts of town.
Yet when I arrived, instead of an elderly kappa, I found in the very small house a kappa of barely twelve or thirteen, whose head-plate had not even hardened, leisurely playing the flute.
Naturally, I thought I must have entered the wrong house.
But when, to make sure, I asked his name, he proved to be none other than the elderly kappa Bag had told me about.
“But you look like a child…” “Don’t you know yet?
By some twist of fate, I already had a head of white hair when I came out of my mother’s womb.
Since then I have gradually grown younger, until now I have become a child like this.
Still, if you count my age, taking me to have been sixty before birth, I may now be around a hundred and fifteen or sixteen.”
I looked around the room.
Perhaps it was only my imagination, but amid the plain chairs and table there seemed to hover a kind of pure happiness.
“You seem to live more happily than the other kappas, don’t you?”
“Well, perhaps that is so.
When I was young, I was old; and now that I am old, I have become young.

p.src: Consequently, I neither thirst after possessions like the old nor drown myself in passion like the young. At any rate, even if my life has not been happy, it must surely have been peaceful.”

u.src: Consequently, I neither thirst after possessions like the old nor drown myself in passion like the young.
At any rate, even if my life has not been happy, it must surely have been peaceful.”

p.src: “I see. Then you must indeed be at peace.” “No, that alone would not have brought me peace. I was also strong and healthy, and possessed enough wealth never to want for food throughout my life. But I still believe my greatest good fortune was that I was already old when I was born.” For a while I talked with this kappa about Tock, who had killed himself, and Gael, who was being examined by a doctor every day. Yet for some reason the elderly kappa wore an expression suggesting that my stories did not interest him very much. “Then unlike the other kappas, you are not particularly attached to being alive, are you?” The elderly kappa looked at my face and quietly replied: “Like every other kappa, before I left my mother’s womb, my father first asked whether I wished to be born into this country.” “But by sheer accident, I tumbled down into this country. Please tell me the way by which I can leave it.” “There is only one way out.” “And what is that?” “The same way by which you came here.” For some reason, this answer sent a shiver through me. “Unfortunately, I cannot find that way.” The elderly kappa fixed his fresh, limpid eyes upon my face. At last he rose, walked over to a corner of the room, and pulled a rope that hung there from the ceiling. At once, a skylight I had not noticed before opened overhead. Beyond that round skylight, past the spreading branches of pines and cypresses, the vast sky shone a deep, cloudless blue. And there, too, towered the peak of Mount Yari, shaped like a gigantic arrowhead. Like a child who has caught sight of an aeroplane, I literally leapt for joy. “Now then, you may leave through there.”

p.src: As he spoke, the old kappa pointed to the rope I had seen earlier. What I had taken for an ordinary rope until then was actually fashioned into a rope ladder. “Then, if you’ll permit me, I’ll leave by way of there.” “But let me warn you beforehand. Be sure you won’t regret it after you leave.” “I’ll be all right. I certainly won’t regret it.” No sooner had I replied than I was already scrambling up the rope ladder, gazing down from far above at the dish on the old kappa’s head.
